title: The Toll
passages:
She didn't take the tag. HOLD stayed flat on the slate, the one refusal the Figure couldn't file, so the Figure did the next thing protocol allowed: it started walking the rows, trailing its copper wire, tag swinging like a pendulum that already knew the answer. Adeyemi's only move that wasn't a refusal was to follow. She took her hand off the stone. HOLD went dull and settled, and behind them the busbar woke an inch for every step.

"Charming," Voss said, limp dragging. "It's walking us to our rooms."

Senn stopped coughing first. They'd been reading cradle plates as they passed, pattern-mad, and the dark ones didn't add up: the rows weren't numbered by position but by filing order. "The price has an address," they said. "002 is at the old end."

The old end was warm. Cradle 002 fogged from inside, seals breathing a slow two-count, and in it a body lay with hands crossed and the fourth mark open on the wrist like a signature still wet. Senn knew the face from the log portraits, the one the voice wore when it wanted to be a person. "Renner. It filed its own name, from in here."

Voss laughed, the cracked note again. "So the count's been paid out of that one cradle."

The sleeper's eyes opened, and they were not Renner's, and when it spoke, it spoke with Adeyemi's voice, because the count had gone through her to get this far: "Three."

The word "Three" lingered in the amber mist, and Adeyemi felt the count shift restlessly behind her sternum. Three cradles. Three breaths given. And 002 was already spent.

Voss's laughter was dry, almost bitter. "Three. The universe really does love a cruel arithmetic." She looked from the dark cradle behind them—the one that went quiet when the toll ran from 002—to the occupied 002 ahead. "Who's the third sleeper we haven't met yet? Who's breath buys this number?"

Senn was already moving, fingertips brushing the slate plates as they passed. "The rows aren't numbered by position," they muttered, pattern-seeing accelerating. "They're numbered by filing order. Three means three names erased. But 002 was already paid." Their mist-body flickered, edges unstable. "Which means someone's been added to the ledger without our knowledge. Or the count is recycling names."

The Maintenance Figure had reached the next cradle down. Its tag hung blank. The slate above it read a name in ink that was already beginning to rewrite itself, wet and uncertain. Not Renner. Not Adeyemi either.

Adeyemi's hand found the slate. HOLD had gone dull when she took her hand off, but she pressed it back to the stone, reasserting the refusal. The amber surged, sharp and sudden. The count faltered. Behind them, the busbar groaned—a sound like metal stretching—and went still for a heartbeat. Then it woke again, ticking upward.

"Adeyemi—" Voss started, but the word was cut as the count shifted: "Three. Four."

And the cradle that answered Four was not the one anyone expected.

The busbar clicked to Four and held. Adeyemi kept her palm on HOLD, but the slate only warmed under her hand, the refusal dulling at the edges like a blade left too long in the sheath. The Maintenance Figure stopped at the dark cradle behind them—the one that had gone quiet when 002 paid its toll. Its tag swung once, twice, then dropped flat against the seal. Ink rewrote itself above the hatch: 004. No name. Just the number.

Voss pushed off the wall, her limp dragging harder, dead fingers twitching at her side. "That cradle was empty," she said. "I saw you close it."

"It wasn't empty," Senn said. Their mist-body was coming apart at the wrists, gray vapor slipping from their sleeves. "It was waiting. Four isn't a row. Four is a return."

The seal hissed open. Inside lay a body—human, whole, dressed in the tech greens Senn wore in the log portraits. Senn reached for it, mist-fingers trailing copper sparks, but the Maintenance Figure stepped between them, wire extended. Adeyemi gripped the copper throat on the Figure's wrist and pulled. Amber surged up her arm, hot and sharp. The Figure froze. Senn stumbled into the cradle. The seals clicked shut. The count held at Four.

Voss stared at the closed hatch. "You just buried them."

Adeyemi let go of the copper. Her hand shook. "No. I gave them a body back. Now we find out if it's theirs."

The seal had barely clicked before Senn's mist-wrists started to fray, vapor leaking into the cold air of the cradle. They ignored it. The body lay on the slab, dressed in tech greens that matched Senn's own portrait in the logs. Whole. Unlimped. Breathing slow and even, chest rising beneath the fabric.

Senn reached out. Copper sparks bled from their fingertips onto the dead metal of the cradle wall. The body's face was Voss's—senior lead Voss, the same Voss limping outside with dead fingers and an amber-fed leg. But this Voss had both legs, both hands, a pulse Senn could feel through the fabric at the wrist. Two of them. One breathing inside the seal, one dying outside it, and the busbar ticking upward between.

"Four wasn't me," Senn whispered. Their pattern-seeing clicked into place, ugly and certain. "Four was her. The count took Voss's breath and left her standing."

Outside, the busbar groaned. Senn pressed both mist-palms against the seal, copper flaring up their arms. The body's eyelids fluttered. Senn made a decision: if Voss's breath was being spent to buy this number, then Senn would spend their own mist-body to break the seal before the busbar reached Five and finished the filing. They shoved against the metal, vapor cracking into static, and the hatch screamed.

The hatch gave with the sound of a bone leaving its socket, and Senn came apart with it. Half their mist-body poured through the gap in a gray sheet, and they dropped against the far wall, wrists gone to static, watching the whole body on the slab sit up like it had only been waiting for the door.

The whole Voss opened both eyes. Clear. Level. She looked at the copper still spitting off Senn's ruined arms and said, in a voice with no drag in it, "You closed the hand. Fourth was mine. I felt it file."

The Voss outside the seal had gone the color of the deck plates. "I'm out here," she said. "I'm the one still breathing."

"You're the one it kept." The whole Voss swung both legs off the slab, steady on feet that had never limped. "I'm the one it spent. There's a difference, and it's about to matter."

Adeyemi's palm was still on HOLD and the slate beneath it had gone from warm to a low, warning heat. What was left of the refusal was a wire, thin and bright and fraying. "Nobody spent anything," she said. "We're all standing right—"

The busbar clicked. "Five."

The chamber dropped to ember-light. Out in the rows the Maintenance Figure turned its blank face and hunted, tag swinging cradle to cradle for a number it could take. But 002 was spent dry and 004 was full and there was nothing left in the rows the count could reach.

The tag stopped. It swung back, slow, and settled on Senn—the only thing in the chamber that had never been given a number.

"There's no empty cradle," the whole Voss said. "So it makes one. It files whatever isn't filed yet."

The limping Voss pushed off the wall before anyone could stop her, dead fingers dragging, amber leg hissing. She put herself in front of Senn and turned her back to the Figure—the one posture the tags can't read. "Then it can choke on me," she said. "I'm done watching it take somebody new."

The Figure's tag swung toward Voss's spine and stopped dead, like a compass finding a wall. It swept left, then right, hunting the number that would let it file her, and found only the flat refusal of her turned shoulders. The amber leg hissed. The dead fingers didn't move. The tag quivered and could not land.

"It can't read her," Senn breathed, half a voice now, static where a throat should be. "Adeyemi. It can't read a back."

Adeyemi didn't answer. Her palm was welded to HOLD by heat, the wire under it burned down to one bright strand. The busbar ticked—not up, not down. Five, and stuck. The whole Voss stood very still, both clear eyes on the frozen tag, and for a second nobody breathed, because a count that can't finish is worse than a count that can.

Then the station decided it didn't need the rows anymore.

Down the chamber, past 002's dry husk, a seal cracked. Then another. Ember-light spilled from cradles that had been dark since before any of them woke, and the breath Five had been hoarding went into them instead—one cradle's worth, spent to buy a workaround. The sleepers were coming up.

The first sat forward out of the frost, coughing station air like it had been holding it for years. Adeyemi knew the face before it finished turning. She knew it because she scraped it every morning in the one working mirror on Deck 2.

"Operator 19," the sleeper said, in Adeyemi's own flat voice, and looked at the palm welded to HOLD. "You're holding it wrong."

"Wrong," the second Adeyemi said, and sat up. Frost came off her shoulders in sheets. "It's not a latch. It's a signature. You sign it every strike or the station re-reads you and finds nothing under its hand." She looked at Adeyemi's palm, blistered, the ink running back toward the knuckles. "It's eating your number to keep that wire lit. You've known that. You stopped reading it."

"Then take it off me." Adeyemi's voice came out wrong. "You want HOLD, come and hold it."

"I do." The second Adeyemi didn't move. "I want the Figure's tag. It names a return occupant, and I'm the only thing in this room it's already filed once. I sign, Five reads me clean, the count finishes where it started—at me—and nobody else in these rows gets woken for the toll." Senn's static laughed once, ugly. "Forty-one strikes ago I signed it and it spent me. You're what it kept."

Behind her the cracked cradles kept opening, and each sleeper sat up looking at her and not at Adeyemi. "Quiet," she said, and thirty faces went quiet. "Operator 19," they all said, in one flat voice, and waited.

Adeyemi looked at the busbar. The wire under her palm had one bright strand left, and the station was reading her off it, over and over, looking for a number. She opened her hand.
